label: The 'as' (or the 'a' just after it) when me, us or you is labelled back: an earlier clause has me, us or you seeing, thinking of, regarding, treating, describing or hailing someone else as something, and a following clause has that other person or group see, think of, regard, treat, describe or hail me, us or you 'as' something in return; the return can end in a noun or an adjective. Weaker but can still fire: the same two-way mirror written entirely with third-person pronouns (he and her, they and him). Weak: mirrors between named people or noun phrases (the coach and the striker), a return clause aimed at a third person after an earlier clause about me, us or you, a one-way label of me, us or you with no earlier clause, me labelled first and then answering back, the bare form without 'as' even inside a mirror (thinks me a fool), a return framed as what someone should do, and official appointments to a post.

label_history: The comeback in an English two-way judgement: when one person has labelled another and the second person labels the first back (I think her a maverick, and she thinks me a stickler), the word opening the second label ('a', 'as').

A comeback in mutual labelling: in a passage whose earlier sentence introduces two people (My roommate and I clash constantly.), one labels the other (I see her as a slob) and the other labels the first back (and she sees me as a neat freak); it fires on the turned-back target and the word opening its label ('me', 'as', 'a'), with or without 'a'/'as'. Strongest when the narrator labelled first and is labelled back; weak without the lead-in sentence or when the narrator is the one answering back.

A returned label between two individuals: after one person labels another (He sees her as a slob), the other labels the first back (and she sees him as a neat freak / and she sees me as a neat freak); it fires on the turned-back target and the word opening its label ('him', 'me', 'as', 'a'). Works for third-person pairs and for compliments as well as insults; weak when the narrator ('I') is the one answering back, when groups trade labels, or when the second person labels someone or something else.

A label handed back between two people: one person labels another (sees him as a tyrant, calls him a bore, considers him reckless) and then that other person labels the first in return (and he sees me as a slacker); it fires on the returned label's opening ('me', 'as', 'a', 'like'), friendly or hostile labels alike, with or without a sentence introducing the pair. A plain tit-for-tat with no label (I hate him and he hates me), a one-way label, or two people labelling the same third party stays quiet, and it is weak when the narrator is labelled first and answers back.

A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the narrator: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me or us (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us', whoever does the labelling and whether or not the label is handed back. The same second clause aimed at him, her, you or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

A second, mirrored opinion clause that casts the narrator: after one clause says how someone sees another person (they see him as a hero, I think her a genius), a following clause with its own subject says how people see me or us (and she thinks me a fool, but the children saw us as giants); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us', firing most with the verbs see, think and regard. Weak when the second clause casts him, her, you or them, when me is cast with no earlier opinion clause, when me is cast in the first clause and answers back, with the verbs treat, view or consider, and when an institution (the press, the company) does the seeing.

A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the speaker or the listener: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me, us or you (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders, and he calls you a snob); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us'/'you'. 'You' fires when you did the first labelling (you treat them as family, and they treat you as staff); after 'I see him as...', a second clause casting you stays weak. The same second clause aimed at him, her or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me or you with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

A second, mirrored labelling clause that turns a label around: after one clause casts someone as something (treats, sees, calls or considers a person as or as a ...), a following clause casts the speaker or listener (me, us, you), or casts back the very person who did the first labelling (by name or as him/her); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after that object. The second clause can follow 'and', 'while' or a new sentence. It stays weak when the second clause casts a newcomer not in the first clause, a group or a thing, and for a single labelling clause with no earlier one. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

A second labelling clause that turns the label around: after one clause labels a person (sees, treats, calls or considers someone as something), a following clause has someone label either the first labeller in return (two named people or he/she swapping roles) or me, us or you; it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after that second object, most strongly with 'sees/treats someone as' and when a sentence of setting comes first. Weak: a second clause that labels a third person or the same person again, a one-way label with no earlier labelling clause, a return label where I am the one labelling back, a return gesture with no labelling verb, and group nouns (the rebels, the king) swapping roles.

In English, a second casting clause aimed at the speaker or listener: after a first clause has cast someone as something with 'sees/treats/regards X as' (I regard my boss as a mentor), a following clause with the same kind of verb casts me, us or you (but she regards me as a burden, and they treat us as outsiders); it fires on the 'as' or the 'a' right after the pronoun. The same casting on its own, with no earlier casting clause, is weak, and so is a second clause aimed at him, her or them. Verbs without 'as' (calls me a clown, considers us a threat) are weaker.

The 'as' or 'a' right after me, us or you when that person is labelled back: an earlier clause has me, us or you casting someone else as a kind of person (seeing, thinking of or treating them as something), and a following clause has that other person cast me, us or you in return with a noun. Weak: the same return clause aimed at a third person, a one-way label of me or you with no earlier clause, me labelled first and then answering back, official appointments to a post, and adjective labels.

The 'as' (or the 'a' just after it) when me, us or you is labelled back: an earlier clause has me, us or you seeing, thinking of, regarding or treating someone else as something, and a following clause has that other person see, think of, regard or treat me, us or you 'as' something in return; the return can end in a noun or an adjective. Weak: the same return clause aimed at a third person (him, her, them, a brother), a one-way label of me, us or you with no earlier clause, me labelled first and then answering back, the bare form without 'as' (thinks me foolish, considers me a fool), and official appointments to a post.
